questions.question_text: Under SB 5191, when must a Washington broker enter a written brokerage service agreement with a buyer?
questions.correct_answer: Before or as soon as reasonably practical after services begin
distractors: Only when writing a purchase offer
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.020(2)(a) requires the firm to enter a written services agreement with the principal "before, or as soon as reasonably practical after, its appointed broker commences rendering real estate brokerage services." SB 5191 extended that long-standing seller requirement to buyers effective January 1, 2024. It is not a hard pre-service deadline, and no services agreement is required for a broker acting as a buyer's agent solely for commercial real estate (RCW 18.86.020(3)).

questions.question_text: A broker drafts a buyer brokerage agreement in Washington. What is the default engagement term under SB 5191?
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.020(2)(b)(i) requires the services agreement to state its term and, for a buyer, "a default term of 60 days with the option of a longer term." Sixty days is the default the form supplies, not a statutory minimum or maximum — the parties may agree to longer.

questions.question_text: A buyer signs a brokerage service agreement that does not address limited dual agency consent. Is this agreement compliant with SB 5191?
questions.correct_answer: No, limited dual agency consent is required
distractors: Yes, dual agency consent is optional
Yes, if the buyer verbally agrees
Only if another form covers it later
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.020(2)(b) requires the services agreement to record two separate consents: (iv) whether the principal consents to the appointed broker acting as a limited dual agent, separately initialed with an acknowledgment of the limits in RCW 18.86.060; and (v) whether the principal consents to the firm's designated broker and supervising managing brokers acting as limited dual agents in an intra-firm transaction. Omitting them makes the agreement noncompliant.

questions.question_text: Which element must be separately initialed in a Washington buyer brokerage service agreement?
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.020(2)(b)(iv) requires the limited dual agency consent to be separately initialed by the principal, together with an acknowledgment that a limited dual agent may not advocate terms favorable to one principal to the detriment of the other. Compensation terms, broker identity, and showing obligations must all appear in the agreement but are not separately initialed.

questions.question_text: A buyer asks their broker to show a home but has not yet signed a written services agreement. Under RCW 18.86.020, what may the broker do?
questions.correct_answer: Show the home if the agreement follows as soon as practical
distractors: Show the home with no agreement ever needed
Show the home only after the buyer makes an offer
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.020(2)(a) requires the written services agreement "before, or as soon as reasonably practical after" the broker commences rendering services — so the broker is not barred from showing the home, but the firm must get the agreement signed promptly. If the buyer keeps refusing, the broker cannot go on providing services indefinitely without one, and RCW 18.86.080(7) means the firm cannot be compensated without a services agreement.

questions.question_text: A broker represents a buyer and learns the seller is offering compensation to buyer agents. Under Washington law, what must the broker disclose?
distractors: Only the listing price to the buyer
Nothing until the buyer makes an offer
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.030(1)(g)(ii) requires a broker to disclose in writing "any terms of compensation offered by a party or a real estate firm to a real estate firm representing another party," before the broker's principal signs an offer or as soon as reasonably practical but before mutual agreement. The duty does not depend on the buyer asking.

questions.question_text: Under Washington disclosure requirements, a broker entering a limited dual agency situation must inform whom?
questions.correct_answer: Both the buyer and the seller
distractors: Only the party they originally represented
Only the designated broker of the firm
questions.explanation: When a transaction involves limited dual agency, the broker must disclose this status to all parties involved. Both buyer and seller must be informed so they can decide whether to consent to limited representation.

questions.question_text: Under SB 5191, what is the new name for the pamphlet brokers must provide to clients?
distractors: Consumer Guide to Real Estate Agency
questions.explanation: SB 5191 replaced the old "The Law of Real Estate Agency" pamphlet with a new one titled "Real Estate Brokerage in Washington," set out verbatim in RCW 18.86.120. It must be formatted so a buyer or seller can easily review it, in a legible font, and it must be provided before the party signs a services agreement (RCW 18.86.030(1)(f)).

questions.question_text: When must a Washington broker provide the 'Real Estate Brokerage in Washington' pamphlet to a prospective buyer?
distractors: Only if the buyer requests it
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.030(1)(f) requires the pamphlet to be given to any party the broker renders services to "as soon as reasonably practical but before the party signs a services agreement," and to any unrepresented party before that party signs an offer.

questions.question_text: A broker gives a buyer the required brokerage pamphlet. What must the broker obtain from the buyer?
distractors: A signed waiver of agency rights
questions.explanation: Washington law requires the broker to obtain written acknowledgment of receipt of the pamphlet. This documents that the consumer received and had the opportunity to review the information about agency relationships.

questions.question_text: The 'Real Estate Brokerage in Washington' pamphlet summarizes the law from which statute?
questions.explanation: The pamphlet is a plain-language summary of chapter 18.86 RCW, prescribed word for word in RCW 18.86.120. It walks the consumer through licensing and supervision, how agency relationships arise for sellers and for buyers, limited dual agency, duration, the required contents of a services agreement, broker duties, and compensation.

questions.question_text: Broker Rivera meets a walk-in client at an open house. The client wants to write an offer immediately. What must Rivera do regarding the pamphlet?
questions.correct_answer: Provide the pamphlet before the agreement
distractors: Skip the pamphlet due to time constraints
Provide it within 48 hours of closing
questions.explanation: Even in time-sensitive situations, the broker must provide the 'Real Estate Brokerage in Washington' pamphlet as soon as reasonably practical and before signing any brokerage service agreement. The requirement cannot be waived.

questions.question_text: Under RCW 18.86.030, when must a Washington broker disclose in writing whom the broker represents?
questions.correct_answer: Before the principal signs an offer
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.030(1)(g) requires written disclosure of whether the broker represents the buyer, the seller, or both as a limited dual agent "before the broker's principal signs an offer, or as soon as reasonably practical, but before the parties reach mutual agreement." It must appear in a separate paragraph titled "Agency Disclosure" in the purchase and sale agreement or in a separate writing with that title.

questions.question_text: A listing broker's seller is offering buyer-agent compensation. Under Washington disclosure requirements, what must the listing broker do?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose compensation offered to other parties
distractors: Share it only if the buyer's broker asks
questions.explanation: RCW 18.86.030(1)(g)(ii) requires written disclosure of any terms of compensation offered by a party or firm to a firm representing another party. Separately, RCW 18.85.361(10) makes it a disciplinary ground to charge or accept compensation from more than one party without first making full written disclosure to all parties.

questions.question_text: During negotiations, a transaction shifts to limited dual agency. When must the broker disclose this change?
distractors: At the time of final closing
Within 10 business days of the change
questions.explanation: A broker must disclose limited dual agency status before providing further services. Washington law requires disclosure before providing brokerage services so that all parties can make informed decisions about proceeding.
